A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AmpleHate and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–C. The retained material and limited additions support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark results, target ablations, convergence measurements, attention visualizations, and error analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains those original empirical results and adds evaluations using a smaller NER tagger and randomly assigned targets.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1–3.3 retain the same target identification, attention-based relation computation, and direct-injection procedure and equations. The additional NER size is an evaluated configuration of the existing method.

E1.justification: Both versions use IHC, SBIC, DYNA, Hateval, Toxigen, White, and Ethos, with individual-dataset and combined-dataset training. The additions introduce no new datasets, tasks, or input scenarios.

E2.justification: Table 3 adds a Random Target comparator to the existing target ablations. BERT, SharedCon, and LAHN remain the comparison methods in Tables 1 and 2.

E3.justification: v3 adds a BERT-base NER configuration and a random-target control with 20% assignment, motivated by approximately 20% explicit-target coverage. Existing splits, classifier backbone, metrics, optimizer, and training budget are unchanged.

E4.justification: Table 1 adds a check of NER model size, while Section 5.1 and Table 3 add random targets to assess the importance of target selection. Existing target ablations, case analyses, attention visualizations, and convergence analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report averages over three random-seed runs. Appendix C retains the same per-run results, standard deviations, and 95% t-based confidence intervals; the added configurations introduce no new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Existing numerical results are retained. Table 1 adds BERT-base NER results averaging 81.21 macro-F1, alongside the unchanged BERT-large NER average of 82.14. Table 3 adds random-target scores averaging 76.71 and stopping steps. Section 4.4 also corrects 'all' to 'nearly all' baselines.

T1.justification: The target definitions, attention and injection equations, and mathematical reasoning are unchanged. Neither version adds formal assumptions, propositions, or proofs relative to the other.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions and claims concerning target-context amplification, human-aligned attention, state-of-the-art performance, and faster convergence.

C2.justification: The explanations of White and SBIC behavior, interpretations of implicit-target attention and convergence, and limitations concerning NER errors, complex sentences, and new domains remain unchanged.

D1.justification: The v3 abstract adds a repository address and states that code is publicly available. Section 3.4 identifies the additional BERT-base NER checkpoint, and Section 5.1 newly reports approximate explicit-target coverage to explain the random-control setting.

R1.justification: The bibliography and related-work discussion retain the same cited works and positioning relative to contrastive learning, target-aware modeling, embedding steering, and attention sinks.

P1.justification: v3 rewrites the abstract opening, expands the ablation description, makes small wording and affiliation edits, and replaces the placeholder acknowledgments with funding information. The section sequence and most prose remain unchanged.

P2.justification: Tables 1 and 3 gain rows and expanded captions, and Table 2 clarifies its tagger configuration. Figures 4 and 5 are repositioned. Appendix prose changes to two columns, with Tables 6 and 7 grouped on the final page; their content is retained.

improvement.justification: The smaller-tagger evaluation and random-target control strengthen scrutiny of NER dependence and target selection, while the code address improves reproducibility information. The corrected comparative wording better matches Table 1. These are limited gains: the core study is unchanged, and the abstract still misleadingly describes the 82.14 macro-F1 average as an improvement over baselines.
